Elden Ring is a good game, but it's so bogged down by its own weight that I don't think I've ever encountered a game that's overstayed its welcome to this degree. 

Prior to playing, I'd read the criticisms of reused content and open world recycling, but I genuinely didn't think it would be as bad as it actually is. You know that meme, where it's [Game] (picture of things clustered together) and [Open World Game] (picture of same things spaced apart)? I don't think that actually captures the dynamic of Elden Ring. That sentiment implies that an open-world game has bespoke, quality content with stretches of empty space between them. In reality, the situation is actually worse in Elden Ring. It's not that there's quality content separated by empty space -- it's actually mediocre content separated by empty space.

So, so, SO much of the content in Elden Ring simply isn't worth doing, at all. Your first Catacomb is worth doing for novelty, sure, but the fifth and tenth one certainly aren't. You will find the same exact enemy types and design principles in every single one -- by having experienced one Catacomb, you have experienced them all (and the first experience, frankly, isn't particularly memorable anyhow). Sadly, Catacombs are actually one of the more interesting POI types in Elden Ring, since they tend to have more involved  layouts and traps. Other POI types, like Caves, are abysmally boring, being indistinct, featureless tunnels, and some, like Ruins, barely qualify as content at all, being literally a staircase into a chest and nothing more. To add insult to injury, rewards are infrequently worth your time, often being a consumable material you have dozens of and a spirit ash no human in history has ever actually equipped to their hotbar. These two things, in tandem, mean that exploring POIs in Elden Ring have neither intrinsic nor extrinsic value -- you don't want to do them for their own sake, and you don't want to do them for the item rewards, either.

The result of this dynamic is that nothing in Elden Ring really feels new past the first area. In them, the majority of things to find are the same stale, bland POIs you've already experienced. Liurnia might as well be Blue Limgrave, Caelid be Red Limgrave, Altus Yellow Limgrave, and so on. While they might be "new" areas, they house the same tired content you've already experienced prior to entering them. In that way, the entire world collapses. Reuse is the name of the game: POIs, enemies, bosses, field enemies. I found myself actively skipping most field content past the 40-50 hour mark. Why make a 80-100 hour game, then, if much of it isn't worth playing? It calls into question the entire open-world format; it's structurally flawed, and Elden Ring is no exception. You have functionally experienced 80% of the gameplay loop by the time you have cleared the Weeping Peninsula.

What about the other 20%, then? Well, the other 20% is some of the best content in video gaming, ever. The legacy dungeons -- the actual quality, bespoke content one might hope to see in a video game -- are truly exceptional. Areas like Leyndell and Nokstella will simply astonish you with their atmosphere, layout, and exploration. These zones are exceptional, and the usual Soulslike successes -- weighty combat, tense experience loss mechanics -- shine as you make your way through these imaginative and exhilarating zones. They evoke fantastical wonder and white-knuckle adrenaline in equal measure.

Legacy dungeons are truly a joy to play through, but they beg the obvious question: why weren't these the whole game? Why did Fromsoft waste so much time on Shitty Cave #20-30 instead of just developing actually good content? Elden Ring feels open world for the sake of being open world -- the structure adds very little, if anything, to the game but takes so much. The opportunity cost of developing at scale is too steep to ameliorate, even for veteran developers with the resources and creative freedom to execute their vision somewhat faithfully. I understand that there's a sense of epicness that comes with a sheer size, but I don't think it was worth it for Elden Ring. The game would be twice as good if it were half the size, filled with content that's actually worth doing. I understand the desire to break away from the Dark Souls brand, but, in my opinion, nothing about the trade was worth it -- especially so since the best parts of the game (like interwoven dungeon layouts, expanded character movesets, and weapon art customizability) are just Dark Souls+.

Ultimately, I do recommend Elden Ring, but with the heavy caveat that it is the victim of its own ambition. The game is too big, too empty, too formulaic for its own good. I do understand why Elden Ring is beloved, and I do understand why it's such a seminal title in gaming. I'll also admit that I've never particularly cared for the open-world format. But I truly believe that, subjective opinions aside, it does more harm than good to Elden Ring. I've played for about 80 hours, enjoyed much of it, and am very near the end of the game, but I simply don't have the stamina to continue. Maybe I'll pick it up again in the future, but the friction is grinding.

There's enjoyment to be had, but be warned: you have a lot of chores to do between the fun.

Don't listen to the gleaming positive reviews of this game: They aren't people who *actually* play soulslike games for fun.

I wouldn't recommend it because:

>It has a major problem with what's known as "twinking" - people abusing the multiplayer mechanics to invade new players. It's not your normal "Oh it's dark souls and I'm getting invaded" - it's legitamately people save-editing in souls or "runes" as ER calls them, dropping high level items for new characters, and so on. This was a problem in Dark souls, yes, but ER it's even worse because they will spawn the invader right next to you - and furthermore, the game isn't as mechanically complex as in Dark souls. So They will just kill you. you can't really fight back unless they're bad. That takes some of the fun out of the concept of "getting invaded".

There are some serious flaws with the game: The exploring to get crafting items feels not very fleshed out and feels like an afterthought to force the player to engage with the open-world aspect, and is more monotonous than adds to the gameplay. None of the crafting items have detailed descriptions so you just have to grab everything not really knowing why. 

The Merchants and so on are generic NPCS - another big gripe with the game, the lack of NPC story characters. And the goods they sell seem completely useless - spells which aren't better than the basic magic bolt yet cost more mana. weapons and armour that are shittier than the starting armor. etc. Only useful shit is the crafting kit and the torch.

Let's talk about the spells and mana: They made the decision to move from spell casts to a mana bar. However, the mana and health system is woeful. Why invest in more mana, more health, when the flasks don't actually replenish it fully? You'll end up finding the next key flaw with the game which revolves around investing in level ups into stat increases.

Essentially: No point in investing in vitality, because don't have enough flasks and not enough flask enhancements. No point in investing in mana for the same reason. 

No point investing in endurance, because you start with SO MUCH STAMINA. Your stamina bar is bigger than both your health and your mana. It comes back so quickly. Investing in endurance does increase equipment load, but you virtually never find any equipment requiring more load so what's the point? 

And so you're just going to be investing in either dex or strength, depending on the scaling of your starter weapon. Another big gripe? Investing in either of those two stats will increase your physical defences across the board in all stats - so what's the point of investing in *both* when I should just invest in whichever one scales the quickest? The outcome: You'll just invest shittons into e.g Dex and basically nothing else.

Next: Let's talk about levelling up, and runes. The enemies in this game drop essentially no runes. The low level enemies are cheap chaff that the game expects you to farm to engage in the open world aspect. The bosses equally drop very little. So why bother? They also don't really drop terrible useful items. You could legitimately just go for the strongest bosses and ignore 80% of the open world - so why on earth would you design an open world with so little depth?

With so few new items, getting new armor or weapons to upgrade seems pointless. It makes you feel unsure about whether or not you're meant to use the smithing stones to upgrade gear. People like choice. And they're more likely to upgrade their gear if they have some idea about whether or not they'll find something better around the corner. You don't have that sort of frame of reference in ER. 

The magic and range in this game sucks for different reasons: As a magic user, or fighting magic users - all of the magic is essentially homing. This is a major deviation form Dark souls games. That makes it infuriating to fight against because you can't just dodge or walk around it - and it takes all the fun out of playing a mage too. There is no point in using a bow because it opens up a clunky ass menu where you have to manually move the crosshair over an enemy - unlike any other game where using a bow is just semi auto-locking but dodgeable ranged attack. 

Let's talk now about the multiplayer co-op: You need to craft these dragon flowers to spend the consumable to do coop and see your friend's summon sign. However this feels really pointless because those flowers are everywhere, and it just means every time you die you've got to use a random consumable that isn't even hard to get. This is clearly *trying* to mimic human effigies in dark souls, but because there's no negative, you don't lose max health when dying or so on, it just feels shallow and monotonous.

Lets talk about the enemies and the bosses: Very few enemies or bosses seem to be unique or have mechanical depth in the combat. So, So many of them are just "I'm a little goblin, I'm small and you can't hit me easily, I'm fast and dart around, I will attack you really fast three times in a row" - and the same sort of goes for the bosses too. you can backstab bosses, which feels sort of neat I guess, but it also makes it less hard and fulfilling. Furthermore, a lot of the bosses you seem to just be able to stun and stop them from attacking you, at least early game. Stunlocking bosses isn't particularly fun. Nor is it fun when *you* get stunlocked by an enemy that attacks quickly and that is *every* enemy. In dark souls, the enemies and bosses had clear movesets, cues to dodge attacks, and combat had mechanical depth. ER doesn't. The biggest exceptions to this seem to be Giants, Kaiden, and the golden sentinel, at least early game. But even then, be prepared for the boss/enemy to spam the same move 17-thousand times.  

The choice between taking health or mana ( flasks are interchangeable) means being a spellcaster is squishy while being a swordsman means you'll never engage with the magic aspect and be a spellsword.

Because all the enemies are so fast, it's deadly to be a greatsword or heavy weapon user - most likely you'll just choose a rogue-like playstyle and stunlock enemies with your quick attacks and your dex build. When there's little choice, the game becomes less fun.

Lets talk about the lore: Where is it? This games lore was made by GRR martin, apparrently, who wrote game of thrones. But in that same way that game of thrones is just incel LOTR for people with ADHD, the lore of Elden ring seems to be all show and no tell. Many of the bosses and npcs and enemies just feel wierd for the sake of it - like how the lore of Dark souls evolved the wierd enemies, ER just saw the wierdness and forgot the Lore was what made it spooky or cool or creepy. The major lack of character NPC's definitely contributes to this, as does the lack of dialogue.

In this game, talking to NPC's doesn't really evolve the same benefits as in Dark souls. THe closest you get early game is some random goblin rat dude who was turned into a tree, gives you a random mushroom you can forage literally anywhere, and later you just find dying outside a cave. Speaking to him literally evolves nothing of value. It's more likely that you'll be forced to speak to the npc's because it will lock you out of the bonfire with no indication that's what you're meant to do.

Let's also talk about the spammy, unhelpful notifications. The game will bombard you with them at the worst of times, and they're awkward to close. Your UI fades by default, and messages stay open on your screen not fading unless you explicitly press a button. They also aren't self-consistent.  sometimes you need to press x button, othertimes they want you to press y, sometimes it's neither (???). No, I don't need to know every single mushroom I pick up for five minutes.

All in All, this title is a Major step BACKWARDS from DS2 - worse than DS3. The deviation encouraged the worst aspects of the title without fixing any of the flaws. The incel community sucks.

There isn't much needed to be said about the positives in regards to elden ring, it's an absolute masterpiece and legitimately one of the best games of our modern times, it's a wonderful game and absolutely worth the experience, I love elden ring and of course I recommend it you'd have to be silly to not do so, that said, after all this time I noticed something in the recent games that probably will never come back...

Fromsoftware games have kinda pivoted from invasion systems to this more chaotic hyper action warzones for multiplayer modes, and as an effect it lost a real spark about how invasions used to function, it engineers a complete shift in mentality for the playerbases for the worse, the gameplay is amazing and the pvp is fun, but it's less of an experience than it ever was, the gameplay is faster, better, more responsive and you have more tools than ever before, but because of the way the entire system was built all you will ever get from multiplayer is the same warzone encounters over and over again, with the same types of players, with the same mentalities, just in a different part of the map.
My complaint is that this shift in perspective on pvp has stolen any organic and variety feelings out of multiplayer, in dark souls remastered you will find people still spamming well what is its until they fall off the map in invasions or all sorts of other stupid shit, from cosplayers to trolls trying to break your equipment, people giving away stuff for the fun of it, griefers getting npcs agroing you and so on and so forth, same for dark souls 2 and even 3 on some level, in elden ring it's kinda always the same. You'll never be invaded by "diabetes type 3" who's using a massive club that looks like a turkey leg who's struggling to walk with equip load over 300% in elden ring, it's not gonna be an absolute fight for the ages but you'd die laughing from the encounter itself, and this sorta interaction was always what made dark souls so magical to me, it was the absolute randomness you'd find with the humans you interact with in these games, but now it's more of a straight minded sort of matchmaking competitive game in elden ring and in the future with duskbloods, it's not wrong or bad in and of itself, again Elden ring is a masterpiece, but I find myself missing that spark from older titles, and if the direction these games are taking is on a more narrow matchmaking mindset, I'd hope some other game or series would take the mantle of invasions in a more organic manner than these newer games.
That said? Of course I recommend Elden ring, it's a masterpiece in all other regards, you don't even need to think about it.

Kind of like the "Anti-Triple AAA" RPG, well, besides the new horse armor. No quest markers, XP trees, quippy dialogue, pride flags, or girl-bosses. Just you vs an entire world that is designed to kill you. Your skill, build, and wits are what will carry you to become the Elden Lord. If you've never played a souls game, this is a good place to start as it can be pretty forgiving compared to the straight cheese of the other titles. Fast travel and short boss runbacks keep the game's difficulty centered on the bosses and areas themselves. 

Regarding mechanics, building out your character is immensely satisfying and addicting. This is one of the most "re-playable" RPG's out there because of the build variety, secrets, and NG+ potential. Deleting a early-game boss in NG+ with your fully-realized build will never get old. Experimenting with different stat spreads and running crazy meme or meta builds is always a great time. The fantastic DLC only builds on this, introducing many new weapons, incantations, armor sets, etc. Technically, the world and it's inhabitants looks amazing and the soundtrack is brilliant. The only gameplay complaint I have is that some enemies repeat a little too much, and the delay on certain boss attacks is just ridiculous. I would also liked to have seen more cutscenes, especially for the endings and DLC bosses.

Overall, this is a must-play for Action-RPG fans and those who are bored of the "movie-game" and "modern audience" tropes. Pickup the SOTE edition and enjoy a game that never really holds your hand and respects your skills and intelligence.

Review after beating the game (65h)

Elden Ring – A master...piece of shit

Elden Ring is a weird game. Beautiful graphics, fantastic combat, incredible world design, yet I spent much of my playthrough wondering whether I was having fun.
The world is full of memorable places, classic FromSoftware gameplay, and some genuinely fun enemies and bosses.
And then there's Torrent. The horse. The legend. The actual secret weapon. Forget legendary swords. Running past 90% of the nonsense is probably the most useful ability in the game.

Elden Ring has two gameplay modes: explore endlessly or git gud.

Exploration becomes exhausting. The world is enormous, yet regular enemies are barely a threat. You spend hours checking every cliff and cave, collecting hundreds of items you'll never use.
Another cookbook? Fantastic. Another crafting material? Just what I needed.
The game makes you explore every edge of the map because maybe something useful is hidden there. Spoiler: usually there isn't. Or it's not what you need.

Then there's the difficulty balance.

Without Mimic Tear, some bosses feel like beating a brick wall with a toothpick. With Mimic Tear, suddenly you're the brick wall. There's little middle ground between getting destroyed and watching your clone do half the work.
I love challenging combat, but I'd rather feel I won than found the unofficial easy-mode switch. 

And finally, the story.

Cryptic lore, depressing characters, dying worlds, NPCs speaking in riddles. Classic FromSoftware. But Elden Ring feels particularly bleak. I never felt like a hero.
The Chosen Undead in DS1 and Ashen One in DS3 weren't traditional heroes either. These games are about struggling through broken worlds. But Elden Ring gave me little reason to care about becoming Elden Lord.

The verdict?

Brilliant ideas, fantastic combat, breathtaking environments, memorable moments.
Also bloated, repetitive, frustrating, and obsessed with rewarding exploration with stuff nobody needs.
When it's good, it's brilliant. When it's bad, you're riding Torrent around another cliff looking for an item you'll never use.

A game I can admire more easily than I can love.
